title: Low-cost soil moisture sensing for smallholder irrigation scheduling: a two-season field trial

headings.text: Low-cost soil moisture sensing for smallholder irrigation scheduling: a two-season field trial

key_sentences: Smallholder vegetable growers in the savanna zone irrigate by habit rather than by measurement.
Over-irrigation wastes pumped water and fuel, while under-irrigation during fruit set cuts yields sharply.
Commercial tensiometers cost more than a season of fuel, so we tested whether a capacitive sensor costing under five dollars could guide irrigation decisions.
Sensor-guided plots received 28 percent less water while yielding slightly more onions.
The saving was largest in the first six weeks after transplanting, when farmers usually irrigate every second day.
The yield gain is modest, but the fuel saving alone repays the sensor within the first month.

list_items.text: Calibrate a low-cost capacitive probe against gravimetric soil samples.
Compare sensor-guided scheduling with farmers’ usual practice.
Measure water use, onion yield and net income per plot.
A five-dollar capacitive probe, calibrated once per soil type, is accurate enough to schedule irrigation.
Sensor-guided scheduling saved over a quarter of the water and fuel without any loss of yield.
Adoption depends on a display that farmers can read at a glance.
